channel.title: Pratik Dhanave — Blog
channel.description: Long-form writing on multi-agent AI, medical AI governance, HIPAA-aware architecture, and cloud-native systems.

item.title: Helping AI Teams Turn Great Demos into Real Production Value
item.description: I'm opening up my consulting, focused on forward deployed engineering for AI and technical teams. One of the most remarkable things about this moment in AI is how quickly an idea becomes a convincing demo — and the most meaningful work is turning that demo into dependable value inside a customer's real environment. Here's the work I'd love to help with, and why it matters to me.

item.title: The Multiplier Mindset: Consulting That Leaves Teams Stronger
item.description: The best outcome of a consulting engagement isn't that the consultant becomes indispensable — it's that the team no longer needs them. The multiplier mindset — amplifying a team's capability instead of creating dependency — is both the more honorable goal and the better business, and it's the heart of forward-deployed work done well.

item.title: The End-to-End AI Financial Engineering Stack
item.description: Having built every piece — data, pricing, risk, ML, documents, underwriting, monitoring, portfolio, governance, memory, production — this closing post assembles the end-to-end stack, shows where value really concentrates (reading, judgment-augmentation, institutional memory — not market prediction), and the principles that tie the discipline together. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Productionizing Financial AI — From Prototype to Trusted System
item.description: A prototype that works in a demo is far from a system an institution trusts with capital. Productionizing financial AI means meeting the reliability, latency, security, and operational bars of a regulated environment where silent failures lose money. The posture: trust is the actual product. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Institutional Memory — Capturing Judgment So It Compounds
item.description: An institution's most valuable asset is its accumulated judgment — why decisions were made, what went wrong last time — yet it lives in people's heads and walks out the door. Institutional memory captures that judgment so it persists and compounds: capture the reasoning, connect decisions to outcomes, retrieve precedent on demand. Perhaps the deepest, most durable value. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Risk Management and Building Models in Practice
item.description: Risk management is the purpose every model served. Value at Risk and its tail-hiding flaw (so expected shortfall), fat tails, hedging with the Greeks, market microstructure as a systems problem, and the overriding lesson: models are approximations that will eventually be wrong — so respect the tails and stay humble. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Operating in Production — Cost, Latency, Incidents, and the Tightening Loop
item.description: Running an LLM app means treating cost and latency as first-class constraints (model routing, token hygiene, caching, streaming), preparing for incidents as certainties (provider failures, instant rollback, blameless postmortems), and the closing idea: operating is continuous improvement — a tightening loop, because an LLM app is never done.

item.title: Model Risk, Validation, and Governance for Financial AI
item.description: In finance, an AI model you can't validate, explain, or audit is a liability and often a regulatory violation. Financial AI inherits decades of model-risk discipline (SR 11-7) and must handle AI's new failure modes (opacity, hallucination, vendor risk). The reframe: governance isn't a tax — it's what makes AI deployable at all. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Randomness — Stochastic Models and Monte Carlo
item.description: Prices are random, so finance is a probabilistic discipline. Brownian motion and geometric Brownian motion model how a price wanders; Monte Carlo simulation turns that model into a universal engine for pricing and risk — the computational core of modern quant finance, and territory engineers find familiar. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Observability and Tracing — Seeing Inside an LLM System
item.description: 'The model messed up' is never a useful diagnosis. Why ordinary monitoring isn't enough, tracing as the spine (spans capturing the rendered prompt, retrieved context, tool calls, raw output, tokens/cost), and turning aggregated traces into metrics, quality trends, and drift detection.

item.title: Portfolio Construction and Aggregation — Seeing the Whole Book
item.description: Individual positions are half the picture; the portfolio is the other half. Construction (what to hold) and aggregation (the firm-wide risk view), why seeing the whole book clearly is deceptively hard, and why AI helps most with consistent aggregation and surfacing hidden concentration — not fancier optimization against unforecastable returns. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Option Pricing — Black-Scholes and the Greeks
item.description: Black-Scholes turned option pricing into engineering: price an option by the cost of continuously replicating it, so no-arbitrage pins its value and the underlying's expected return drops out entirely. Risk-neutral valuation, what the model assumes, implied volatility, and the Greeks traders actually hedge. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Guardrails and Safety in Production — Containing Open-Ended Output
item.description: An LLM can say anything, which is the problem. The new failure modes — hallucination, prompt injection, data leakage, harmful output — and layered, fail-closed guardrails (input, output, action) with humans in the loop, treated as part of the lifecycle and red-teamed.

item.title: Credit and Position Monitoring — Watching the Thesis Over Time
item.description: Monitoring is the long aftermath of a deal — watching whether the thesis still holds as the world changes. AI makes it continuous: reading every update, tracking every covenant, flagging variance from the thesis the moment it appears — attacking the classic failure of problems noticed too late. The make-or-break is signal over noise. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Derivatives and the No-Arbitrage Principle
item.description: A derivative's value derives from something else — and it's priced not by prediction but by the no-arbitrage principle: if a portfolio replicates a payoff, it must cost the same. Forwards, futures, options, payoff shapes, and the replication argument that prices a forward and links calls to puts. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Online Evaluation and Feedback — Production Is the Real Test
item.description: Offline evals say a change is safe to ship; online evals say whether it worked. The intrinsic offline–online gap, deploying to measure (canary, A/B, shadow), capturing explicit and implicit feedback, and the pipeline that turns production behavior into continuous improvement.

item.title: AI Underwriting — From Deal Materials to Auditable Judgment
item.description: Underwriting turns deal materials into a decision — slow, manual, judgment-heavy work and a flagship AI application. Turning raw materials into structured, pressure-tested, auditable analysis: reading the deal record, surfacing risks, pressure-testing against precedent, drafting IC docs — while judgment stays human and everything stays traceable. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Risk and Return
item.description: Higher expected return requires more risk — and the surprising twist is that diversification reduces risk for free when assets are imperfectly correlated. Volatility, covariance, the efficient frontier, systematic vs. idiosyncratic risk, and how CAPM prices risk through beta. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Eval-Driven Development — You Can't Ship What You Can't Measure
item.description: The practice that separates improving an LLM app from merely changing it. The curated eval set as the core asset, how to score open-ended output (deterministic checks, reference metrics, LLM-as-judge, human review), and how to gate every change on evals and compare B vs A.

item.title: NLP and LLMs on Financial Documents — Reading at Scale
item.description: Finance runs on documents — filings, memos, indentures, contracts — and LLMs can finally read them at scale. The most consequential capability in AI financial engineering, and the discipline it requires: grounding, provenance on every output, hallucination defense, and human verification. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Bonds and the Yield Curve
item.description: A bond is the simplest real application of discounting: fixed future cash flows, priced by present value. From there come yield, the inverse price-yield relationship, duration and convexity as interest-rate risk, and the yield curve as the market's price of time. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Prompt and Version Management — Treat Prompts Like Code
item.description: In an LLM app the prompt is the source code — where behavior is defined and most bugs happen. Treat prompts like code: version the whole configuration (template + model + parameters + context strategy), decouple them from app code, and route every change through review, eval, rollout, and rollback.

item.title: Forecasting Markets and Financial Time Series
item.description: Predicting where markets go is the most attempted and humbling problem in finance. Why financial series are especially hard (near-efficiency, noise, non-stationarity, fat tails, reflexivity), what can actually be forecast (volatility over direction, distributions over points), and why the goal is risk, not alpha. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Building a Forward Deployment Function
item.description: A practical blueprint for founders: when to start forward deployment, who to hire first, how to scope engagements, what to measure, and how to keep it from eating your margins — plus the four failure modes (agency, hero, science-project, over-serving) and a 90-day start.

item.title: The Time Value of Money
item.description: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow — and that single fact, made precise, is how everything in finance gets valued. Present value, future value, discounting, and the discounted-cash-flow method that prices anything with a future payoff. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: The LLMOps Lifecycle — The Loop an LLM App Lives In
item.description: The LLMOps lifecycle — develop, evaluate, deploy, observe, improve — as a loop an LLM app lives inside, not a line it runs once. Why evaluation is a first-class stage appearing twice, why production feedback flows backward, and why the loop turns whether you act or not.

item.title: Machine Learning in Finance — What Works and What Doesn't
item.description: Finance is the hardest domain to apply ML to — noisy, non-stationary, adversarial — and the ways to fool yourself are endless. An honest guide: where ML genuinely works (information, structure, credit, computation), where it reliably fails (market prediction), and why the discipline is mostly not deceiving yourself. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: The Forward Deployed Leader
item.description: Forward deployment that isn't run as a disciplined function becomes an unscalable custom-dev shop. The Forward Deployed Leader owns the motion as a business — team design, scoping discipline, unit economics, and the decision of what becomes product — and names the invisible trap: it feels like success right up until the margins invert.

item.title: What Financial Engineering Is
item.description: Financial engineering applies math, statistics, and computation to money — and under the jargon it rests on three ideas an engineer will recognize: the time value of money, the trade-off between risk and return, and no-arbitrage. This series builds quant finance from those foundations. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: What LLMOps Is — and Why It's Not Just MLOps
item.description: Getting an LLM to work in a demo is easy; keeping it working, safe, and affordable for a year is a discipline. What LLMOps is, how it differs from MLOps, and the five properties of LLMs — opaque external models, prompt-defined behavior, fuzzy correctness, non-determinism, new failures/costs — that force a different playbook.

item.title: Risk Engines in Production — Quantifying What Could Go Wrong
item.description: The risk engine answers what keeps institutions solvent: what could go wrong, and how badly? Building VaR, stress testing, and scenario analysis in production, how AI accelerates (surrogate-powered scenarios) and extends (unstructured risks) — and the danger it carries: AI can make risk engines more confident and more wrong at once. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: The Forward Deployed Architect
item.description: The forward deployed engineer builds a win inside one customer; the Forward Deployed Architect makes it survive the next ten — reference architecture, security and governance that passes review, and the reuse decision that separates product from one-off. The missing layer between heroics and product.

item.title: Profiling and the Optimization Workflow — Measure, Don't Guess
item.description: You can't optimize what you haven't measured. The optimization loop — baseline, profile, find the dominant limit, apply the matching lever, repeat — plus knowing when to stop, leaning on the ecosystem, and the durable mental model behind it all.

item.title: Pricing and Valuation Engines — Building the Core
item.description: At the heart of most financial systems is an engine answering 'what is this worth?'. Building valuation engines in production, and where AI fits: accelerating expensive computations (ML surrogates for Monte Carlo) and extending valuation into illiquid, document-driven instruments. Engineered to be validated, auditable, and reproducible. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: The Forward Deployment Stack
item.description: The forward deployed engineer gets all the attention, but forward deployment is bigger than one role — it's a go-to-market operating model with three layers: build (engineer), scale (architect), run (leader). Seeing the whole stack is how AI companies turn embedded engineering from a heroic cost center into a repeatable engine.

item.title: Memory Management for LLM Inference — The KV Cache Problem
item.description: The KV cache often exceeds the model weights in HBM, and naive contiguous allocation wrecks concurrency with fragmentation. PagedAttention applies operating-system paging to fix it — a core inference bottleneck solved by borrowing a classic systems idea.

item.title: The Data Foundation — Where Financial AI Lives or Dies
item.description: Every financial AI system lives or dies on its data, and financial data is uniquely treacherous: expensive, fragmented, revised, survivor-biased, and riddled with ways to accidentally see the future. The landscape (market, document, proprietary data) and the traps — lookahead, survivorship, point-in-time correctness — that make it the most decisive part. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: The Attention Bottleneck — and How FlashAttention Fixed It
item.description: Naive attention materializes an N×N matrix in HBM — memory-bound and quadratic. FlashAttention fixes it with pure roofline reasoning: tile into shared memory, use an online softmax, fuse the kernel, never touch HBM. The archetype of all inference optimization.

item.title: What AI Financial Engineering Is — Where Quant Finance Meets AI
item.description: Financial engineering has always been computational; AI now extends it into reading documents, structuring judgment, and monitoring risk. What AI financial engineering is — the synthesis of model-driven quant and data-driven AI — and why finance (real money, mandatory explainability, auditability, adversarial data, human judgment) makes it uniquely hard. (Educational, not financial advice.)

item.title: Numeric Precision — Why Lower Precision Makes Inference Faster
item.description: FP32, FP16, BF16, and INT8/INT4 — how a float splits bits between range and precision, why bf16 won, and why fewer bits is a double win: less data to stream from HBM and faster tensor-core math. Quantization and why LLMs tolerate it.

item.title: The Skill Reference — Structure, Templates, and Putting It Together
item.description: The concrete reference: the anatomy of a skill definition (the SKILL.md pattern — metadata/trigger, instructions, knowledge, resources), starter templates (general, domain, workflow, integration), and the series' synthesis — make agents reliably useful by building and tending a library of captured expertise.

item.title: The CUDA Execution Model — Threads, Warps, and Occupancy
item.description: Threads, warps, blocks, and grids; SIMT and branch divergence; and the cleverest trick — hiding slow memory by oversubscribing warps (occupancy). Why a GPU can be underutilized without being either compute- or memory-bound.

item.title: Skills in the Wild — What Works in Real Use
item.description: The gap between a demo skill and one that works in daily use is where the real lessons live. What makes skills succeed in the wild (the fundamentals), the failure modes that recur (drift, overlap, trigger misfires, bloat, over-trust), and operating the library as a maintained, curated, shared system.

item.title: From Bespoke AI to Product
item.description: Every AI FDE builds one-offs — a bespoke deployment for one customer's data, workflow, and trust. The ones who create lasting value turn those one-offs into product: the patterns that repeat become a platform, the platform makes the next deployment faster, and field learnings flow back to shape what gets built. The flywheel that turns bespoke AI work into a compounding asset — and the AI FDE career arc.

item.title: The Roofline Model — Are You Compute-Bound or Memory-Bound?
item.description: The roofline model answers the one question that governs every optimization — compute-bound or memory-bound? — from arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte). Why LLM prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound, and why batching is the master throughput lever.

item.title: Domain-Specific Skills
item.description: Domain-specific skills capture deep field expertise — law, finance, a specific codebase, a regulated process. The highest-value and highest-stakes skills, demanding the most rigor: grounded authoritative knowledge (not the model's hallucinations), precisely-stated rules, verification, and human oversight.

item.title: Productionizing and Handing Over AI
item.description: A pilot that works is not a system the customer can run. Productionizing AI means making it reliable, affordable, fast, and observable enough to be real infrastructure — then handing it over so the customer operates it without you. The FDE's goal, in the end, is to make themselves unnecessary. Cost, latency, drift, observability, and a handover that transfers the eval discipline, not just the code.

item.title: The Memory Hierarchy — Why Bandwidth Rules Inference
item.description: The GPU memory hierarchy from registers to HBM, the difference between capacity and bandwidth limits, and the defining fact of LLM generation: it's memory-bandwidth-bound because every token reads the whole model from HBM — which is why batching and quantization work.

item.title: General Business Skills
item.description: The highest-value skills often capture ordinary recurring work — a standard document, a review process, a routine analysis. Their failure mode is being too generic; the value is entirely in your specifics. Why frequency-times-people makes them high-leverage, and how to find them.

item.title: Integrating AI into Real Workflows
item.description: A technically excellent AI system that nobody uses has delivered zero value. The last mile of an AI deployment is not the model — it's fitting the system into how real people actually do their jobs, designing an interface that handles uncertainty honestly, and managing the human change of introducing AI into someone's work. Human-in-the-loop, calibrated reliance, autonomy levels, and change management.
